questions.question: In a common-value auction with value $v$ and private signals $\theta_i$, what does the winner's curse refer to?
options: Every winner overpays, even in equilibrium, because value estimates are noisy
Naive winners overpay by bidding $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]$, ignoring what winning reveals
Winners overpay because each bidder's estimate of $v$ is biased upwards
Winners of private-value auctions regret paying more than rivals' values

questions.question: In a common-value auction with symmetric bids that increase in the signal, why is winning ‘bad news’ for a bidder about the common value $v$?
options: She wins only by paying more than the others were willing to pay
Winning shows that her bid exceeded her own unbiased estimate of $v$
Her own signal is biased upwards, so her estimate of $v$ is too high even before she wins
She wins when her signal is the highest, so the others' signals were lower

questions.question: In a Bayesian Nash equilibrium of a common-value auction, do winning bidders lose money on average because of the winner's curse?
options: No: rational bidders condition on winning, so winners do not lose on average
Yes: overpayment by the winner is a built-in feature of every equilibrium of such an auction
Yes, unless the auction is a second-price auction with truthful bids
No, because in equilibrium all bidders bid their naive estimate $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]$

questions.question: Bidders in an auction may have private values or a common value. Why does the winner's curse not arise in an auction with private values?
options: With private values all bidders have the same valuation
With private values the winning bidder always pays exactly her own value
A rival's signal carries no information about one's own value
With private values bidders know the rivals' valuations

questions.question: Each of $n\ge2$ bidders estimates a common value $v$ by $\theta_i=v+\varepsilon_i$, with i.i.d. errors of mean $0$ that are not always $0$. Which statement about the estimates is correct?
options: Each $\theta_i$ is unbiased, but $\max_i\theta_i$ overstates $v$ on average
Each $\theta_i$ overstates $v$ on average, so all bidders are too optimistic
The largest estimate $\max_i\theta_i$ is unbiased because the errors average out
Each $\theta_i$ is unbiased, so the winning estimate is unbiased too

questions.question: In which of the following auctions is a winner's curse most likely, given that each bidder forms her own estimate of the object's worth?
options: A painting each bidder wants for her own home, valued by her own taste
A seat at a concert, valued by how much each bidder likes the band
Drilling rights to an oil field of unknown size, estimated by surveys
A meal voucher each bidder values by her own hunger that day

questions.question: The object's common value is $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$, where $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ and bidder $i$ observes only $\theta_i$. Bidder 1 observes $\theta_1=0.3$. What is her naive estimate $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.3]$, which ignores any information in winning?

Three bidders estimate a common value $v$ by $\theta_i=v+\varepsilon_i$ with i.i.d. errors $\varepsilon_i\sim U[-20,20]$, and each bids her estimate in a first-price auction. What is the probability that the winner pays more than $v$?

Two bidders estimate a common value $v$ by $\theta_i=v+\varepsilon_i$, where the errors are independent and equal $+10$ or $-10$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each. What is $\mathbb{E}[\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)]$, the average overshoot of the larger estimate?
In a common-value auction, how does adding more bidders affect a rational bidder's downward adjustment for the information in winning, and her equilibrium bid?
options: The adjustment grows, but competition pushes bids up, so the effect on bids is model-dependent
The adjustment shrinks, since with many bidders each single signal matters less for the estimate of $v$
The adjustment grows, so equilibrium bids always fall whenever more bidders are added
Neither changes, since the adjustment depends only on her own signal, not on the number of rivals

questions.question: In the symmetric equilibrium of a second-price common-value auction (highest bid wins and pays the highest rival bid), which expected value of $v$ should bidder $i$ with signal $\theta_i$ bid?
options: $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]$, her unconditional estimate
$\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ \text{all rival signals}=0]$
$\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ \text{highest rival signal}=\theta_i]$
$\mathbb{E}[v\mid\text{highest rival signal}]$, ignoring her own signal

questions.question: Bidders' estimates of a common value are $\theta_i=v+\varepsilon_i$, $i=1,\dots,n$, with i.i.d. mean-zero errors. In which case is the largest estimate $\max_i\theta_i$ an unbiased estimate of $v$?
options: When $n=1$, or when the errors are always exactly $0$
Whenever the error distribution is symmetric around $0$
When $n$ is very large, so that the errors average out
Whenever the errors are uniform on an interval symmetric about $0$

questions.question: The object's common value is $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$, where $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ and bidder $i$ observes only $\theta_i$. Under the first-price rule (the highest bid wins and is paid) the symmetric equilibrium bid is $b(\theta)=\theta$. Bidder 1, with $\theta_1=0.8$, wins when $\theta_2<0.8$. How much profit does she expect conditional on winning?

Bidders observe noisy signals of a common value $v$. Suppose the seller gives the object at a fixed price to a bidder chosen by lottery, independently of all signals. Why is there then no winner's curse?
options: The fixed price always equals the common value $v$, so the chosen bidder never overpays
Lotteries turn the common value into a private value for each bidder
Signals become unbiased once bids no longer decide the winner
Being chosen reveals nothing about rivals' signals, hence nothing about $v$

questions.question: The winner's curse rests on the logic that ‘the event that the trade happens is informative’. In which situation does the same logic apply?
options: A buyer pays more for a painting she likes more than other buyers do
Two firms choose quantities and the price falls when both produce more
A bidder in a second-price private-value auction bids her own value
A used-car offer is accepted only by sellers whose car is worth less

questions.question: The object's common value is $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$, where $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ and bidder $i$ observes only $\theta_i$. In a first-price auction (highest bid wins and pays her bid) both bid naively $\theta_i+0.5$. Bidder 1 wins when $\theta_2<\theta_1$. What is her ex ante expected profit, averaged over both signals before they are drawn?

The object's common value is $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$, where $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ and bidder $i$ observes only $\theta_i$. In a first-price auction (highest bid wins and pays her bid) both bid naively $\theta_i+0.5$, so bidder 1 with signal $x\in(0,1]$ wins when $\theta_2<x$. For which of these signals is her expected profit given winning negative?
options: Only $x>\frac{1}{2}$, as optimistic signals overstate the value
Every $x<1$, with loss $\frac{1}{2}(1-x)$ shrinking as $x$ rises
Only $x<\frac{1}{2}$, as pessimistic signals win only against weak rivals
No signal, since $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1]$ is an unbiased estimate
